records.title: Mumbai Metro Line 3: from opening to a usable journey
records.scope: One integrated Mumbai Metro Line 3 project, counted once across its staged openings. Depots, station contracts and financing packages add no separate identities; other Mumbai metro lines are outside this account.
records.answer: Line 3 has reached reported full-line operation. The harder question is how its stations, transfers and daily service turn that infrastructure into dependable journeys.
records.stage: Operating line reported; sustained passenger reliability and distributional outcomes not established by this review

identity_decision.rationale: The defined identity is the single Line 3 corridor delivered through successive stages, not three projects created by opening ceremonies. Its depot and station packages remain components. The retained inventory and prior additions contain no counted Line 3 identity; the wider Mumbai place is a separate geographic account, not another project.

timeline.event: The final segment was inaugurated; the government also announced Mumbai One.
JICA reported the full line operational following the previous day's inauguration.
Parliament received a line-specific status, delay and cost account.

sections.heading: An opening is an important, bounded milestone
sections.text: JICA's October 2025 account describes a 33.5-kilometre line with 27 stations, implemented by Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation. Its inventory specifies 26 underground stations and one above ground. That detail is more useful than repeating a simplified all-underground label. The final opening connects an integrated corridor rather than creating another project. For a passenger, however, the relevant service includes the station entrance, the wait and the exit connection; a completed railway is only one part of that journey.

sections.heading: The cost history belongs beside the achievement
sections.text: The December 2025 parliamentary answer lists Line 3's original cost at ₹23,136 crore, revised cost at ₹37,276 crore and escalation at 61 percent. It identifies depot-related decisions and litigation, tree permissions, environmental clearances and the pandemic among delay factors. These are the ministry's reported figures and explanation, not a new independent audit. They warrant a project-specific account: readers should not import the cost, completion year or agency of another Mumbai metro line from an adjacent table row.

sections.heading: Accessible design needs an availability record
sections.text: JICA describes accessible platforms and women-only cars among the line's design features. These provisions matter, but they answer a design question rather than showing whether an accessible route works every day. A useful follow-up would record lift outages by station and duration, identify the alternative path, and show whether staff assistance was available during the outage. This is an editorial test to pursue, not a claim that such failures were observed or that disabled passengers were consulted for this article.

sections.heading: Transfers have their own physical constraints
sections.text: The parliamentary answer identifies connections with suburban rail, including CSMT and Mumbai Central, and a skywalk connection at Santacruz. Naming an interchange does not measure the effort of using it. Our next comparison should follow a complete transfer: walking distance, road crossings, level changes, queuing and the cost of the onward service. Those measurements would help distinguish a connection on a network diagram from a practical connection for someone carrying luggage, travelling with children or unable to use stairs.

sections.heading: One app is not proof of one seamless fare
sections.text: The government's October 8 announcement includes Line 3 in Mumbai One, presented as an integrated ticketing app across eleven public transport operators. That is evidence of the announced product and participating network, not a successful purchase or refund test. The editorial question is whether a particular multi-operator journey can be planned, paid for and recovered after disruption. App availability should therefore be checked separately from fare integration, missed-connection protection and alternatives for passengers who cannot rely on a smartphone.

sections.heading: Measure the service passengers actually receive
sections.text: The next operating account should combine scheduled and delivered trips over a defined period with cancellations, headway variation and station-level accessibility. Ridership needs a dated denominator, while travel-time comparisons need the same endpoints and time of day. A forecast of daily demand cannot fill either role. These measures should be published with their exclusions and disruption days, not reduced to an opening-day success claim. Until that evidence is inspected, this article recognizes the operating milestone without assigning a reliability score or claiming citywide congestion relief.

next_artifacts: A dated Line 3 operating report linking scheduled trips, delivered trips and disruption intervals over the same reporting period.
Station-specific accessible-route and interchange observations, including outage duration and alternative paths.
A documented Mumbai One multi-operator purchase, disruption and refund policy; no live transaction is claimed here.

records.title: Dhaka MRT Line 6: what the early outcomes can tell us
records.scope: One MRT Line 6 corridor in Dhaka, counted once across its construction, financing and extension stages. Loan tranches and other proposed MRT lines are not additional identities. This review does not certify the latest extension's commissioning.
records.answer: Line 6 offers evidence beyond an opening ceremony: research on nearby road speeds and reported household benefits. Those findings describe different populations and periods, not a current systemwide performance score.
records.stage: Operating corridor documented; latest extension status and current reliability remain unverified in this bounded review

identity_decision.rationale: MRT Line 6 is one named rail project with successive financing and implementation stages. The fifth ODA loan does not add a fifth project, and the other planned corridors used as research controls are not counted here. No retained portfolio or earlier cohort identity overlaps this defined line.

timeline.event: JICA signed the fifth project loan agreement; the next day's release retained a future completion schedule.
Commercial operation of the initial section began, the starting point used in the road-speed study.
A separate household-panel study was presented at a development conference.
JICA published a visit account mentioning MRT Line 6, not a service-performance report.

sections.heading: Finance has a different clock from operation
sections.text: JICA's March 2022 agreement identifies Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited as executing agency and provides a fifth loan of up to ¥18.285 billion. That is one financing tranche, not the total cost of the line. The release's December 2025 completion schedule was a forecast made before initial passenger operation, not proof of later acceptance. A useful project chronology must retain that distinction: financing agreements explain how construction was supported, while commissioning and operating records establish what subsequently became usable.

sections.heading: The road-speed study measures a local effect
sections.text: Yamada and Jiang's February 2025 discussion paper uses Google Maps estimated road journeys from 2022 through June 2024. Its event-study comparison contrasts the Line 6 corridor with control corridors. The authors report a short-term speed improvement of roughly 10–15 percent, with some effects declining over time. This is a localized road result, not an estimate of faster trains or relief across all Dhaka. The paper is explicitly not peer-reviewed and expresses its authors' analysis rather than an institutional verdict.

sections.heading: A fading effect is a question, not a failure verdict
sections.text: The paper suggests that additional traffic demand may offset some initial congestion relief and calls for a longer observation period and alternative distance boundaries. Those limitations shape the next research question: does improved access persist even when road speeds stop improving? That question should not be answered with a single traffic indicator. Nor should the paper's June 2024 endpoint be silently extended through later disruption or used to describe November 2026 service. Its original observation window remains visible here.

sections.heading: Household benefits are not evenly distributed
sections.text: A JICA account of a January 2026 conference describes a separate panel of about 4,000 households observed from early 2023 to early 2025. The presentation reported longer, faster trips and lower per-kilometre costs for longer commutes, while noting that low-income women seldom used the metro. Those distributional findings deserve attention alongside corridor speeds. However, this article inspected the conference account, not the underlying household paper or microdata; it does not combine the two studies into a single causal estimate or claim that every household benefited.

sections.heading: A current visit does not settle extension acceptance
sections.text: JICA's July 21, 2026 visit report mentions MRT Line 6, supplying a later dated institutional account than the early research window. It is not a station-opening instrument or a daily operating log. In this review, DMTCL's exact public status pages returned retrieval errors, so no fresh extension percentage or timetable is inferred from search extracts. That access limit does not establish that an extension is unfinished. The next account needs an accessible operator artifact identifying the stations actually open and its effective date.

sections.heading: Build a service and inclusion account together
sections.text: A worthwhile next edition would place observed train intervals and cancellations beside access costs, transfers and the experiences of people who do not use the line. The sample should identify income, gender, trip purpose and distance from stations without presenting a nearby household as automatically served. Fare comparisons need a common journey and include the feeder leg. These are proposed evidence tests, not new survey results. They would connect operational consistency to the distribution of benefits while keeping the rail project distinct from a claim that the city's transport problem is solved.

next_artifacts: A DMTCL station-by-station opening or extension commissioning artifact with its actual effective date, plus the current service timetable.
A defined-period operator record of trips, intervals, cancellations and accessible-station service; the road study cannot substitute for it.
The underlying household-panel paper and its methods, followed by a longer-window congestion study with explicit spatial sensitivity checks.

records.title: Greater Mumbai: connect the railway to the street
records.scope: The Greater Mumbai municipal area served by Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, counted as one place. It is not the whole Mumbai Metropolitan Region; Thane, Navi Mumbai and other neighbouring municipalities are not silently included.
records.answer: Greater Mumbai's transport story is bigger than a new railway. Municipal streets, climate risks and budgeted works determine whether a regional network can become a useful local journey.
records.stage: Municipal planning and budget instructions inspected; delivered neighbourhood outcomes not established

identity_decision.rationale: This account uses the defined municipal jurisdiction, not a national orientation or the entire metropolitan travel market. Regional operators appear as interfaces, not as evidence that their whole service areas lie inside BMC. No ward, suburb or neighbouring municipality is counted again as a child place within this addition.

timeline.event: Reference year of the greenhouse-gas inventory later used by the municipal climate plan.
Climate-plan edition sets out the municipal planning and vulnerability framework.
Date printed on the budget circular requesting revised and next-year estimates.
Mumbai One was announced across a network wider than this municipal boundary.

sections.heading: Keep the municipal boundary visible
sections.text: This article follows Greater Mumbai as a local service jurisdiction, while recognizing that passengers cross its boundary. It does not add Thane or Navi Mumbai to BMC's responsibilities simply because a trip or an app reaches them. That distinction makes comparisons more honest: a regional railway opening, a municipal footpath project and a household journey have different footprints. The practical unit for a future local assessment should be a named station approach or neighbourhood, with the responsible bodies identified for each part of the route.

sections.heading: Climate exposure changes what access means
sections.text: The 2022 climate-plan summary connects transport access with flood, heat and other vulnerabilities rather than treating distance to a station as sufficient. Its framework is a planning basis, not a fresh inspection of any particular route. For a station approach, the useful question is whether the walk remains possible during rain and heat, including for people with reduced mobility. An access claim should therefore retain the hazard assumptions and identify the path being assessed, rather than converting a mapped catchment into an observed dependable journey.

sections.heading: The emissions baseline is historical, not a metro result
sections.text: The plan reports a 2019 inventory in which transport accounts for 20 percent of municipal emissions and stationary energy for 72 percent. Those figures describe the baseline's sector composition; they do not quantify the emissions saved by Line 3. An updated comparison would need consistent geographic and accounting boundaries, electricity assumptions and an observed travel response. Keeping the baseline year attached prevents a historical planning figure from appearing to be a current score or an attributable railway benefit.

sections.heading: The climate budget asks for work, not just ambition
sections.text: The budget circular's English climate annex links departmental requests to action tracks, including public transport, walking and cycling, flood resilience and water services. Its template asks for the work, responsible unit, estimated cost and quantified next-year outputs. That creates a useful route from a broad objective to a checkable item such as a named footpath. It remains a preparation instruction: an entry in a request is not a final appropriation, a payment or an accepted asset that residents can use.

sections.heading: A fleet target needs a service denominator
sections.text: The same annex lists complete bus electrification for 2026–27 as a target. It does not provide an observed fleet count or show how many buses deliver service on a typical day. To assess progress, the next municipal account should distinguish vehicles procured, accepted, available and actually operated, with charging downtime and scheduled mileage alongside them. These are editorial reporting requirements, not newly collected fleet findings. Counting a purchase as a completed low-emission journey would skip both the maintenance dependency and the passenger's experience.

sections.heading: Regional ticketing still meets local streets
sections.text: Mumbai One's launch announcement names metro, suburban rail and bus operators, including BEST and several neighbouring municipal services. The app therefore illustrates a network larger than this place account, not a unified local authority. Its stated digital features do not establish usable crossings, accessible transfers or an affordable combined fare. For Greater Mumbai, the next practical comparison should connect one end-to-end journey to the relevant street works, operator rules and disruption arrangements, while retaining non-digital access as a separate question.

next_artifacts: A final municipal climate-budget work list linked to actual expenditure and acceptance records for named walking, crossing or drainage improvements.
A dated BEST fleet and service account distinguishing orders, accepted vehicles, daily availability and delivered mileage.
A station-approach assessment with exact municipal boundary, route, hazard conditions and responsible agencies, linked to the separate Line 3 account.
